source_text: Verum et his, inquit, tamquam hominibus pepercisti, et misisti praecedentes exercitum vespas; non quia impotens eras in pugna impios iustis subicere, sed partibus iudicans dabas locum paenitentiae. Aculeis, inquit, muscarum etiam illos ipsos sacrilegos stimulabas, ut potentiam vindicantis de ludicro suae afflictionis adverterent. Sed postquam ex consilio Dei, et ultionis genere voluntaria peccata patuerunt, quorum reiectio exspectabatur et petebatur; tunc demum in obstipam punitorum profanitatem scriptoris assurgit invectio, dicitque illos tantam inisse cum criminibus familiaritatem, ut innata quodam modo viderentur. Non ignorans, inquit, quoniam nequissima fuerit natio illorum, et naturalis malitia ipsorum, et quoniam non poterat commutari cogitatio eorum in perpetuum; semen enim erat maledictum ab initio; nec timens aliquem, veniam dabas peccatis illorum [n199] . Cum, inquit, tu tam benigne tamque patienter et paenitentiae tempus indulseris, et speculam admonitionis infixeris, ut iustitiam ac misericordiam ab omni infamia, ab omni suspicione crudelitatis assereres; tamen illi spreverunt commonitiones tuas, qui beneficia praemissa despexerant, velut qui velint probare de illius esse semine Cham, in quem Noe beatus nuditate derisa, censura patria fuerat maledicta iaculatus. Quid ergo mirum, si maioris eorum proterviae merito, sententiae erat austeritate perculsus, recordatus est scriptor in maculam posterorum non desistentium ab aemulatione, cum frequenter in lege imitatio posterorum necessitudinis quoque vocabulis arguatur? Sic quippe Dominus in Evangelio ad Iudaeos: Vos, inquit, ex patre diabolo estis [n200] . Et Daniel contra spurcos presbyteros, de Israel tamen stirpe venientes, eodem genere legitur invectus: Semen, inquit, Chanaan, et non Iuda [n201] . Ezechiel quoque propheta exprobrat plebi Ierusalem: Mater tua, inquit, Cetthaea, et pater tuus Amorrhaeus [n202] . Est ergo hic usus ut ad voluntatis invidiam infamatio stirpis accedat, nimiumque crimini videatur adhaerere, per cuius meritum convicium patiuntur et semina. Servatur autem hic idem mos etiam in bonorum parte, ut cum videtur homo per omnia probus, congenitis dicatur florere virtutibus. Unde et beatus Iob misericordiae affectum quo subveniebat indigentibus, de uberibus se traxisse, immo de utero matris suae secum confirmat egressum [n203] . Nihil ergo rebus perspicuis, aut similitudo, aut exaggeratio, aut ambiguitas praeiudicare potest; quoniam cum certum sit numquam naturalium rerum correctionem a mortalibus reposci, praecipiat autem Deus ut desistant homines a malo; omni vero verius approbatur, naturale peccatum non esse posse.
pass_a_gloss: But even to these, he says, as to humans you spared, and you sent wasps going before the army; not because you were powerless in battle to subject the impious to the just, but judging by parts you were giving a place of repentance. By the stings, he says, of flies you were stimulating even those very sacrilegious ones, so that they might notice the power of the avenger from the sport of their affliction. But after from God's counsel, and from the kind of vengeance, voluntary sins were plain, whose rejection was being waited and asked; then at last the writer's invective rises against the stubborn profanity of the punished, and he says they had entered so great a familiarity with charges that they seemed in a certain way inborn. Not ignorant, he says, that their nation was most worthless, and their natural malice, and that their thought could not be changed forever; for it was a seed cursed from the beginning; nor fearing anyone, you were giving pardon to their sins. When, he says, you so kindly and so patiently both indulged a time of repentance and fixed a lookout of admonition, that you might assert justice and mercy from all infamy, from all suspicion of cruelty; nevertheless they despised your warnings, who had looked down on the benefits sent ahead, as those who would want to prove they are of that seed of Ham, against whom blessed Noah, his nakedness having been mocked, had hurled a paternal censure of curses. What therefore wonder, if by the desert of their greater shamelessness he was struck by the austerity of the sentence, the writer remembered it as a stain of posterity not desisting from rivalry, when frequently in the law the imitation of posterity is also accused by words of kinship? For thus the Lord in the Gospel to the Jews: You, he says, are from your father the devil. And Daniel against filthy elders, coming nevertheless from the stock of Israel, is read to have inveighed in the same kind: Seed, he says, of Canaan, and not of Judah. Ezekiel the prophet also reproaches the people of Jerusalem: Your mother, he says, was a Hittite, and your father an Amorite. There is therefore this use that an infamation of stock accede to the spite of will, and it seems to cling too much to a charge, through whose desert even seeds suffer insult. But this same custom is kept also on the side of goods, that when a human seems proven through all things, he is said to flourish with virtues born-with. Whence also blessed Job confirms that the affection of mercy by which he was helping the needy he drew from the breasts, nay went out with him from his mother's womb. Nothing therefore can prejudge clear matters, either likeness, or exaggeration, or ambiguity; because when it is certain that a correction of natural things is never demanded from mortals, but God commands that humans desist from evil; by every truer thing it is approved that a natural sin cannot be.

pass_b_english: “Yet even these,” he says, “you spared as human beings, and sent wasps ahead of the army—not because you lacked the power to subject the impious to the righteous in battle, but, judging little by little, you gave them room for repentance” (Wisdom 12:8–10). “You pricked even those sacrilegious people,” he says in effect, “with the stings of flies, so that from the trivial instrument of their affliction they might recognize the avenger’s power.” After God’s purpose and the form of punishment made clear the voluntary sins whose rejection was awaited and sought, only then does the writer’s rebuke rise against the stubborn impiety of those punished. He says they had entered into such familiarity with crimes that these seemed in a way inborn. “You were not ignorant,” he says, “that their race had been most wicked, that their malice was natural, and that their thought could never be changed; for they were a cursed seed from the beginning. Nor did you grant pardon for their sins out of fear of anyone” (Wisdom 12:10–11).

He means: “Although you so kindly and patiently granted time for repentance and set up a watchtower of warning, to defend your justice and mercy against every slander and every suspicion of cruelty, they nevertheless despised your warnings after despising your earlier benefits.” They acted as though wishing to prove that they came from the seed of Ham, against whom blessed Noah, after his nakedness was mocked, had hurled curses in fatherly judgment (compare Genesis 9:20–27). Why be surprised, then, that the writer recalled the severe sentence that had struck their ancestor for his insolence, to disgrace descendants who did not cease imitating him? In the Law, imitation by descendants is frequently rebuked using terms of kinship. Thus the Lord says to the Jews in the Gospel, “You are from your father the devil” (John 8:44). Daniel is also read rebuking the filthy elders, though they came from Israel’s stock, in the same way: “Seed of Canaan, not of Judah” (Daniel 13:56; Susanna 56). The prophet Ezekiel likewise reproaches the people of Jerusalem: “Your mother was a Hittite and your father an Amorite” (Ezekiel 16:3, 45).

This is therefore an established usage: defamation of ancestry is added to blame of the will. A person appears to cling excessively to crime when, because of that crime, even his seed suffers insult. The same custom is also observed on the side of good people: when a man appears upright in every way, he is said to flourish with inborn virtues. Thus blessed Job affirms that he drew from the breasts the compassionate feeling with which he helped the needy, or rather that it came with him from his mother’s womb (Job 31:18). No comparison, exaggeration, or ambiguity can therefore count against plain facts. It is certain that mortals are never required to correct natural properties, yet God commands human beings to desist from evil. It is thus proved with the utmost truth that natural sin cannot exist.

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
